abstract: Plasma membrane integrity is essential for cellular survival, yet how cells repair micron-scale plasma membrane ruptures remains poorly understood. Here, using the genetically tractable Caenorhabditis elegans epidermis, we combine live imaging, genetics, super-resolution microscopy, and biophysical approaches to define a size-dependent role for endosomal sorting complexes required for transport (ESCRT)-III in large-scale membrane repair. Small wounds induce transient, focal VPS-32 accumulation, whereas large wounds trigger the formation of a persistent but dynamic, circumferential ESCRT-III assembly that remains associated with the wound during repair. Formation of this assembly requires conserved ESCRT regulators, including ALX-1, TSG-101, and VPS-4, together with VPS-32 polymerization. The wound-associated ESCRT-III assembly is required for membrane tension restoration and efficient membrane repair, while disrupting VPS-32 polymerization impairs tension recovery, reduces vesicle recruitment and wound closure, and consequently compromises axon regeneration and organismal survival following injury. Together, our findings suggest that large plasma membrane wounds induce a persistent, dynamic ESCRT-III assembly that restores membrane tension and facilitates vesicle-mediated membrane addition to promote wound repair.
